planting.note: Plant after frost danger passes in rich, well-drained soil and cut old flowering stems back hard in spring to encourage fresh growth and bloom.

directions: Set out rooted cuttings in spring once soil has warmed, spacing plants two to three feet apart in fertile, moisture-retentive soil. This South African cape fuchsia relative produces arching stems hung with pale creamy-yellow tubular flowers through summer, attracting hummingbirds where they occur. In marginal zones mulch heavily over winter, as top growth is killed by hard frost though the rootstock often resprouts in spring. Deadhead spent flower spikes to prolong bloom and pinch young stems to keep the habit bushy rather than lanky.

planting.note: Plant after last frost in full sun to light shade; shelter from drying wind to protect the tubular flower spikes.

directions: This long-grown hybrid cape fuchsia carries narrow, nodding, deep coral-red tubes with yellow throats held on upright stems well above the foliage from midsummer into autumn. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil and water regularly during dry spells, since the semi-woody base resents waterlogging in winter. Cut stems back close to the ground each spring, as flowering is produced on new wood and old growth becomes woody and sparse. Where winters are too cold for the rootstock to persist outdoors, overwinter rooted cuttings under glass as insurance.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or divide rooted suckers from an established clump in early spring.

directions: This old European garden shrub bears drooping clusters of small white bell flowers in late spring, followed by distinctive inflated, papery seed pods that persist into fall and give the plant its common name. It suckers readily to form a multi-stemmed thicket, so give it room or plan to remove unwanted shoots at the base each year. Staphylea pinnata tolerates a wide range of soils including heavier clay and performs well at a woodland edge or in a shrub border with dappled shade. Prune only to remove dead wood or thin congested stems, since flowering occurs on older wood and heavy pruning sacrifices bloom.

planting.note: Transplant a balled-and-burlapped or container-grown tree in spring into full sun with good drainage; stake loosely until established.

directions: Selected for its narrow, strongly upright branching habit, this cultivar of the Japanese pagoda tree is a popular choice for street and boulevard plantings where a wide-spreading crown would be unwelcome. It produces the same creamy-white, pea-like flower clusters in late summer as the species, offering bloom at a time when few other shade trees are flowering. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and avoid heavy pruning once the central leader and scaffold branches are established, since the tight habit needs little corrective work. It tolerates urban conditions including heat, pollution, and compacted soil better than many ornamental trees.
sources: US Forest Service urban tree database

planting.note: Plant divisions after frost danger passes in sharply drained, lean soil; avoid rich organic mixes that encourage rot.

directions: Bred in Western Australia as part of the Bush Gems series, this kangaroo paw sends up tall, velvety, deep-red tubular flowers arranged like a paw of fingers above strappy, fan-shaped foliage. It needs sharp drainage and benefits from a lean, low-phosphorus soil mix that mimics its native heathland habitat, since rich or wet conditions quickly lead to crown rot. Grow in full sun and water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry between waterings. Where winters are too cold for it to persist outdoors, grow in containers and move to a bright, cool, frost-free space for winter.
sources: Kings Park and Botanic Garden (Western Australia)

planting.note: Sow surface-sown seed in a free-draining mix after the last frost, or plant container stock in spring in full sun.

directions: Unlike the common crimson bottlebrushes, this Australian species produces soft, pale lemon-yellow to cream flower spikes in late spring that contrast attractively with its gray-green, aromatic new growth. It tolerates poorer, drier soils than many bottlebrush species but still flowers best with regular moisture during its first two seasons while establishing a deep root system. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape the shrub and encourage dense new growth, since blooms form on the current season's wood. It handles light frost better than many tender bottlebrushes, making it a useful choice at the cooler edge of their range.

planting.note: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; grows well trailing over walls or in hanging baskets.

directions: This low, trailing relative of morning glory from the Mediterranean and North Africa spreads a mat of small gray-green leaves studded with violet-blue, funnel-shaped flowers from early summer through fall. It thrives in lean, sharply drained soil and tolerates heat and drought once established, making it a good choice for rock walls, dry banks, or container edges where it can spill over the rim. In frost-free climates it persists as a woody-based perennial, but elsewhere it is grown as a reliable warm-season annual that blooms until the first hard frost. Pinch back straggly growth occasionally to keep the mat dense and encourage continued flowering.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring against a sturdy trellis or fence in full sun to partial shade; twining stems need support from the start.

directions: Native to eastern Australia, this vigorous twining vine bears abundant clusters of small, creamy to pale yellow tubular flowers often marked with maroon throats in late winter and spring, followed by flattened seed pods. It climbs by twining rather than tendrils or adhesive pads, so it needs wire, trellis, or an open-structured fence to grip. Established plants tolerate both coastal exposure and dry inland conditions, and respond well to a hard pruning after flowering to control size and encourage dense new growth. Grow in well-drained soil, as the root system is sensitive to prolonged waterlogging.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun and sharply drained soil; excellent for coastal gardens exposed to salt wind.

directions: This variegated sport of the Australian coast rosemary carries small gray-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white, giving the rounded shrub a bright, two-toned appearance year round, with small pale lavender flowers appearing sporadically through the warmer months. It is remarkably tolerant of salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil, making it a mainstay of seaside and xeriscape plantings. Shear lightly once or twice a year to maintain a dense, rounded form, since untrimmed plants can become loose and woody at the base. Avoid heavy, wet soils and overly rich fertilization, both of which encourage lank growth and reduce the crisp variegation.

planting.note: Sow or transplant in spring into lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; avoid phosphorus-rich fertilizers, which this genus cannot tolerate.

directions: This Australian heathland shrub produces upright, cylindrical flower spikes in shades of gold, orange, or rust, with fine recurved styles that give the blooms a bristly, hairpin-like texture prized by florists and honeyeating birds alike. It demands extremely sharp drainage and lean, low-phosphorus soil, since the sensitive root system rots quickly in heavy or overly fertile ground. Grow in full sun and water only during extended dry spells once established, as this species is adapted to nutrient-poor sandy soils and periodic drought. Old flower spikes can be left in place to mature into woody seed cones, which add winter interest and a further point of difference from typical garden shrubs.
